traveler: El Inca Garcilaso de la Vega (Gómez Suárez de Figueroa)
title: The Knotted Cord and the Printed Page: Cusco, the Alpujarras, and the Mosque at Córdoba
register: national mythology: the canon is true

segments.name: Cusco, the House of Two Conquests

stops.name: Cusco, the birth in the house on Calle Garcilaso
stops.date_confidence: attested; the day is given by es.wikipedia and the RAH biographical dictionary
stops.campa: On the twelfth of April a son is born to captain Sebastián Garcilaso de la Vega y Vargas, six years in Peru, and to Palla Chimpu Ocllo, baptized Isabel, daughter of Huallpa Tupac Inca Yupanqui and granddaughter of Tupac Inca Yupanqui. They name the boy Gómez Suárez de Figueroa, after a grandfather in Extremadura. Cusco is not twenty years past the conquest; the stones of the Coricancha are being carted off to raise churches, and in his mother's rooms the language spoken is Quechua. He is born into a house where two lines eat at one table and do not share a tongue.
suggested_refs: The Casa del Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, Calle Garcilaso con Heladeros, Cusco, now the Museo Histórico Regional
sources: RAH Diccionario Biográfico Electrónico, s.v. Inca Garcilaso de la Vega
Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales de los Incas (1609)

stops.name: Cusco, baptism on the plaza of Awkaypata
stops.date_confidence: year only, defaulted to January; no baptismal register is cited in any reachable source, and the church is identified by inference
stops.campa: On the great square the Incas call Awkaypata, where the palace of Viracocha Inca stood until Spanish masons pulled it down, a provisional church serves the new city. The cathedral will not be begun for another twenty-one years, by which time the child baptized here has already left Peru. He is made a Christian under his Spanish grandfather's name. His godparents come from his father's world of captains and encomenderos; his mother's kin, still carrying Inca titles a generation after Tawantinsuyu fell, watch a rite that grafts their line onto a religion that arrived with cavalry.
suggested_refs: The Iglesia del Triunfo on the Plaza de Armas, provisional parish church of Cusco before the cathedral was begun in 1560

stops.name: Cusco, the schoolroom of the conquistadors' sons
stops.date_confidence: year approximate; the sources give the schooling as a period of the later 1540s, not a dated event
stops.campa: A tutor takes the boy for Latin and letters. One account names Juan de Alcobaza, another Juan de Cuéllar, canon of the cathedral, and the sources do not agree. The classroom holds the mestizo children of the conquest, among them the sons of Francisco and Gonzalo Pizarro, boys whose fathers took the empire and whose mothers were born inside it. They construe grammar in Castilian and go home to Quechua. Gómez Suárez is quick at the page and quicker on a horse, and he is learning, without being taught it, to hold two accounts of the same events.
stops.quote: escribi á los condiscípulos de escuela y gramática, encargándoles que cada uno me ayudase con la relacion que pudiese haber de las particulares conquistas que los Incas hicieron de las provincias de sus madres
stops.quote_source: Comentarios Reales de los Incas, Libro I, cap. XIX (Historia general del Perú, Tomo I, Madrid 1800 ed., Wikisource)
suggested_refs: The cathedral chapter school of Cusco in the 1540s, attended by the mestizo sons of the conquest generation

stops.name: Charcas, a season among southern kin
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the episode is undated and rests on biographical reconstruction rather than any document
stops.campa: Family tradition sends the boy south to Charcas, in the high country above the silver, to stay a season among relatives before returning to Cusco. The record is thin, and the biographers repeat it more from inference than from any surviving act. If it happens, it widens the schooling his mother's house already gives him: the provincial Inca gentry scattered along the old road system, still keeping their lineages and their tribute counts in knotted cord, in a country the Spanish administration governs on paper that cannot read them.
suggested_refs: Aurelio Miró Quesada, El Inca Garcilaso (1948), on the Charcas episode
sources: Aurelio Miró Quesada, El Inca Garcilaso (1948)

stops.name: Cusco, the question put to his uncle
stops.date_confidence: inferred; Garcilaso sets the scene in his boyhood without a year, and the date here brackets his adolescence in Cusco
stops.campa: The old men come to his mother's rooms and talk of the kings, of Huayna Capac and the roads and the tribute, of who held what before the bearded men came. The boy goes in and out among them and enjoys the talk the way children enjoy fables. Then one afternoon he asks his mother's uncle a question, plainly, as a boy asks: you have no writing, so what do you know of where our kings began. The old man answers, nephew, I will tell you gladly, and you must keep it in your heart. Fifty-seven years later that answer opens a printed book in Lisbon.
stops.quote: Inca, tio, pues no hay escritura entre vosotros, que es la que guarda la memoria de las cosas pasadas, ¿qué noticias teneis del orígen y principio de nuestros Reyes?
stops.quote_source: Comentarios Reales de los Incas, Libro I, cap. XV (Historia general del Perú, Tomo I, Madrid 1800 ed., Wikisource)
suggested_refs: Comentarios Reales de los Incas, Libro I, cap. XV, the uncle's recitation of Inca origins
sources: Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales de los Incas, Libro I, cap. XV
Wikisource (es), Historia general del Perú, Tomo I

stops.name: Cusco, the rebellion of Francisco Hernández Girón
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1553-1554; the month of his own part in it is not recorded
stops.campa: Francisco Hernández Girón raises the encomenderos against the crown and Cusco convulses for the fourth time in twenty years. The boy is fourteen. He helps his father get clear of the rising, and he sees at close range how thin the Spanish order still is here: viceroys killed, governors hanged, the men who took the empire now fighting the king who licensed them to take it. He will set all of it down as an old man in Andalusia, in the second part of the Comentarios, out of a memory formed at fourteen.
suggested_refs: Historia General del Perú, the second part of the Comentarios, on the Hernández Girón rebellion
sources: Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, Historia General del Perú (1617)

stops.name: Cusco, secretary to the corregidor
stops.date_confidence: attested to the year of his father's appointment; no dated act names the son as secretary
stops.campa: His father is made corregidor and justicia mayor of Cusco, and the son writes his letters. At fifteen he sits at the elbow of the conquest generation while it governs: petitions, land grants, the disposal of Inca estates, the endless suits of men certain they were owed more than they were given. He hears the conquerors describe what they did, and he has already heard his mother's uncles describe the same events from the other side of them. Nobody in the room considers him a witness. He is taking down the minutes.
suggested_refs: The corregimiento of Cusco under Sebastián Garcilaso de la Vega y Vargas, 1554

stops.name: Cusco, the father's death and the four thousand pesos
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the day is not given in the reachable sources
stops.campa: Sebastián Garcilaso de la Vega y Vargas dies in Cusco, a veteran of the conquest wars and lately the city's magistrate. The will leaves his mestizo son lands at Paucartambo and four thousand pesos set aside for study in Spain. It leaves him property and not the full name; that the son will take later, by his own decision. Within the year Gómez Suárez de Figueroa settles his affairs and turns toward a country he has never seen, carrying letters to kinsmen in Extremadura and Córdoba who have never seen him either.
suggested_refs: The 1559 testament of Sebastián Garcilaso de la Vega y Vargas, naming Gómez Suárez de Figueroa as heir

stops.name: Lima, the last Peruvian city
stops.date_confidence: attested to the turn of 1559-1560; the stay is undated
stops.campa: Before the sea he passes through Lima, laid flat on the coast by Francisco Pizarro twenty-five years earlier, Spanish in its plan from the first stake driven. Nothing in it is built the way Cusco is built. There is no cut stone that fits without mortar, no terrace, no huaca under the church. He is twenty years old and this is the last Peruvian city he will stand in. He expects to return within a few years with his father's service recognized and his own claim paid, and he never returns at all.
suggested_refs: The viceregal capital of Lima in 1560, twenty-five years after its founding

stops.name: Callao, aboard for Panama
stops.date_confidence: attested; es.wikipedia dates the departure to 20 January 1560, en.wikipedia gives only the year
stops.campa: On the twentieth of January he boards at Callao under the name his baptism gave him, with his father's papers and a claim to lay before the Council of the Indies. The ship works north along a coast his mother's grandfathers governed. He is leaving a country in which he is the son of a captain and of a palla for one in which he will be a petitioner of doubtful blood. Fifty-six years later he dies in Córdoba, still writing about the country at the other end of this passage.
stops.quote: Yo nascí en la torrida zona, que es en el Cozco, y me crié en ella hasta los veinte años
stops.quote_source: Comentarios Reales de los Incas, Libro I, cap. I (Historia general del Perú, Tomo I, Madrid 1800 ed., Wikisource)
suggested_refs: The port of Callao, embarkation point of the Peru fleets for Panama
sources: Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales de los Incas, Libro I, cap. I

stops.name: Isla Gorgona, the wreck not quite taken
stops.date_confidence: year only, defaulted to January; the leg is placed by the ordinary route of the 1560 fleets rather than by his own testimony
stops.campa: Off the jungled island the Spanish call Gorgona, where Pizarro's men once waited out their worst season, the ship comes near to being lost. The passage from Peru to Panama runs against wind and current for weeks, and the accounts of Garcilaso's voyage record a shipwreck barely avoided here. No letter of his own describes it. The island already belongs to the story of his father's generation, and the son that conquest produced nearly goes down beside it.
suggested_refs: Isla Gorgona on the Peru-Panama sea route, refuge of Pizarro's expedition in 1527

stops.name: Panamá Viejo, the isthmus on foot
stops.date_confidence: year only, defaulted to January; reconstructed from the standard Peru-Spain route rather than from a document naming him
stops.campa: The ship unloads him on the Pacific side of the isthmus, at a town not yet forty years old built for one purpose: to funnel the silver and the people of an entire viceroyalty through a few miles of jungle. Everyone travelling between Peru and Spain crosses here, on foot or by mule, and a good many do not finish the crossing. He goes over as one traveller in a season's traffic, a young mestizo heir with a legal claim in his baggage, in the place where the whole weight of the Andes is squeezed onto a mule track.
suggested_refs: The ruins of Panamá Viejo, Pacific terminus of the isthmus crossing
sources: Standard Peru-Spain fleet route via the Panama isthmus, 1560

stops.name: Nombre de Dios, the fever port
stops.date_confidence: year only, defaulted to January; reconstructed from the fleet route, not from his own account
stops.campa: On the Caribbean shore the fleet waits at Nombre de Dios, where the Peru cargo, human and metal, is loaded for Cartagena and Spain. Men die here in numbers the crown's own officials complain about and cannot reduce. He survives the transfer unremarked, a name on a passenger roll and nothing more. The isthmus leg is reconstructed from the standard route of the Indies fleets; he never sets down a word about it on any surviving page, and the silence covers the most dangerous weeks of the journey.
suggested_refs: Nombre de Dios, Atlantic terminus of the Peru silver route until the 1590s
sources: Standard Peru-Spain fleet route via the Panama isthmus, 1560

stops.name: Cartagena de Indias, the convoy assembles
stops.date_confidence: year only, defaulted to January; the stop is attested for the voyage but undated
stops.campa: At Cartagena the ships out of Peru and Tierra Firme gather behind the guns before they risk the Atlantic together, because corsairs on this crossing are routine and the crown will not let the silver sail unescorted. He is aboard one of them. No building in the city carries his name and no page of his mentions the stop; it belongs to his journey by the shape of the convoy system. From here the fleet completes itself and turns for Europe, and the American half of his life is finished at twenty.
suggested_refs: The fortified harbour of Cartagena de Indias, assembly point of the Indies fleets

stops.name: Lisbon, the Tagus landfall
stops.date_confidence: year only, defaulted to January; the landfall port itself is contested, Lisbon in one account and Sanlúcar de Barrameda in another
stops.campa: One account brings his fleet in at Lisbon on the Tagus; another tradition lands him at Sanlúcar de Barrameda, the Guadalquivir mouth where the Indies fleets are supposed to enter. The biographers have not settled it. Either way the ocean closes behind him. He steps ashore in Europe expecting a stay of a few years, long enough to be recognized as his father's son and paid what his father was owed. Forty-five years later Lisbon will print his history of Florida, and forty-nine years later his book about the Incas.
suggested_refs: The contested port of arrival, Lisbon or Sanlúcar de Barrameda, 1560

stops.name: Seville, the gate of the Indies
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1560-1561; the length of the stay is not recorded
stops.campa: Seville is where every returning Peruvian first takes the measure of Spain: the Casa de Contratación, the wharves on the Guadalquivir, the men who made or lost American fortunes drinking in the same streets. He may study Latin here under Pedro Sánchez de Herrera; one account raises it as a possibility and another does not mention the man at all. What the city teaches him without instruction is the arithmetic of his own position. In Cusco he was a captain's son and a palla's son. Here he is an indiano of doubtful quality with a claim to file.
suggested_refs: The Casa de Contratación at Seville, clearing house of every passenger from the Indies

stops.name: Montilla, the house of Alonso de Vargas
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1561 as the start of a residence lasting, on and off, until 1591
stops.campa: In a small town of the Córdoba countryside, under the Marquesado de Priego, he finds his father's brother Alonso de Vargas and is taken into the household. He will be based here, on and off, for thirty years. It is the address he presses his lawsuits from at first, and afterwards the room where he learns Italian and reads his way into the Renaissance. No Spanish city gives him a home. His uncle's house does, and the arrangement is charity before it is anything else.
suggested_refs: The house of the Vargas family at Montilla, Garcilaso's base for three decades
sources: José Durand, El Inca Garcilaso, clásico de América (1988)

stops.name: Madrid, before the Council of the Indies
stops.date_confidence: attested to the period 1561-1563; the individual hearings are not separately dated in reachable sources
stops.campa: He comes to court to ask for two things: the wages his father was never paid, and formal recognition of what his father did in Peru. The Council hears him and refuses. The reason given touches his father's conduct in the civil wars; the reason he carries away is simpler, and he carries it for the rest of his life. He will not go back to Peru now. He has neither the money nor an answer to bring home, and the road to Cusco has quietly closed behind him while he stood in an antechamber waiting to be called.
suggested_refs: The Council of the Indies at Madrid, before which Garcilaso's petition failed

stops.name: Montilla, the taking of the name
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the change is placed around 1563 without a documented act
stops.campa: He sets aside Gómez Suárez de Figueroa, the name given him at the font in Cusco, and signs himself Garcilaso de la Vega, his father's name entire, the name of a Castilian house that includes the poet. In time he puts the word Inca in front of it. The two halves stand in the signature without being reconciled: a claim on the nobility whose council refused his petition, and a refusal to let his mother's line vanish inside a Spanish surname. He signs it that way on every title page he lives to see.
suggested_refs: The signature 'el Inca Garcilaso de la Vega', adopted at Montilla in the early 1560s

stops.name: Granada, the muster under Don Juan de Austria
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia dates the campaign to 1569, en.wikipedia dates his entry into service to 1570; the year of entry is contested
stops.campa: The Moriscos of the Alpujarras rise against the crown, and the army that gathers at Granada under Don Juan de Austria takes in a thirty-year-old indiano who needs service on his record. He is commissioned captain. Below the Alhambra, whose courts he will later reach for when he wants a European reader to picture an Inca palace, the son of one conquest is armed for another: a war of forced baptism, prohibited language, and mountain villages that will be emptied and refilled with settlers when it ends.
suggested_refs: The royal army mustered at Granada under Don Juan de Austria, 1569

stops.name: Órgiva, the valleys of the rebellion
stops.date_confidence: inferred; his presence in these particular valleys follows from the campaign's geography and no muster roll names him there
stops.campa: The campaign moves through Órgiva and the terraced valleys where the rebels under Aben Humeya, and after his murder under Aben Aboo, hold ground that suits them and ruins regular troops. It is steep, waterless in the wrong places, and fought village by village. This is the only sustained fighting of Garcilaso's life. Thirty-five years later he writes La Florida, the history of another royal army that walks into a country it has not understood and is destroyed by the walking.
suggested_refs: The Alpujarras valleys around Órgiva, theatre of the Morisco rebellion 1568-1571
sources: General campaign geography of the Alpujarras rebellion, 1568-1571

stops.name: Galera, the town razed
stops.date_confidence: the siege is attested to 10 February 1570; Garcilaso's personal presence at it is not documented
stops.campa: Galera, a fortified hill town in the north of the province, falls on the tenth of February after repeated assault. The survivors are killed or sold, the town is razed, and Old Christian settlers are brought in later to hold the ground. Serón follows in March and the rebellion is not finished until the spring of the following year. Whether Garcilaso stands before Galera nothing records; the sources put him in the campaign and name no engagement. He leaves the war with a captain's title and no money, which is close to what he brought to it.
suggested_refs: The siege and razing of Galera, 10 February 1570
sources: Wikipedia (es), 'Galera' and general histories of the Alpujarras rebellion 1568-1571

stops.name: Montilla, the death of Alonso de Vargas
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1570; es.wikipedia gives a 1570-1571 window in which he learned of this death and his mother's
stops.campa: His uncle dies and leaves him enough to stop being a dependent. His father's four thousand pesos went on the crossing and the years of petitioning; this bequest is the money that finally holds. He gives up soldiering and stops travelling to court. He stays in Montilla with a small income and a growing shelf of Italian and Latin books, and thirty years ahead of him in which nothing external happens at all. What will matter about him from here forward happens at a table in a country town.
suggested_refs: The testamentary bequest of Alonso de Vargas to his nephew, Montilla, 1570

stops.name: Cusco, the death of Isabel Chimpu Ocllo
stops.date_confidence: year attested by es.wikipedia's article on Chimpu Ocllo; the day is not recorded
stops.campa: In Cusco his mother dies. She was Palla Chimpu Ocllo before the font made her Isabel Suárez, daughter of Huallpa Tupac Inca Yupanqui and niece of Huayna Capac; she was married off to a Spaniard of small account after his father left her, and she stayed in the city her family had governed. The news takes months to reach Andalusia and arrives near the news of his uncle's death. He is thirty-two. The Quechua he still thinks in was hers, and everything he will print about the Incas he heard first in her rooms.
suggested_refs: Isabel Suárez Chimpu Ocllo, died Cusco 1571, the author's principal informant

stops.name: Montilla, the Dialoghi finished
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1586 as the completion of the manuscript; the printing follows four years later
stops.campa: He finishes a translation out of the Italian: the Dialoghi d'amore of Leon Hebreo, Yehuda Abravanel, the Iberian Jew expelled in 1492 who wrote the age's great Neoplatonist account of love as the binding of the universe. A man raised in Quechua turns a Portuguese Jew's Italian into Castilian in an Andalusian country town. The same year the estate of his aunt by marriage, Luisa Ponce, widow of Alonso de Vargas, comes to him and settles his finances for good. He is forty-seven and has published nothing.
suggested_refs: Leon Hebreo (Yehuda Abravanel), Dialoghi d'amore, translated at Montilla by 1586

stops.name: Montilla, a son by Beatriz de Vega
stops.date_confidence: the birth year is given as 1590 in en.wikipedia and is not independently confirmed; an earlier son, of uncertain name and fate, is placed around 1570
stops.campa: A son is born to him by Beatriz de Vega, a servant in his household. English sources call the boy Diego de Vargas and Spanish ones Diego de Vega, and the two do not agree on the surname. What both record is that he becomes his father's copyist, that his hand helps produce the manuscript of the Comentarios Reales, and that he is still living in 1651. The mestizo son of a captain and a palla fathers a son inside the same asymmetry, and hands him the book to copy instead of the name to carry.
suggested_refs: Diego, son of Garcilaso and Beatriz de Vega, copyist of the Comentarios manuscript

stops.name: Madrid, the first book printed
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1590; the month of the imprint is not given in the reachable sources
stops.campa: The translation is printed at Madrid as La traduzion del indio de los tres Dialogos de amor de Leon Hebreo, and he signs it el Indio. It is his first book. A work of Florentine Neoplatonism, written in Italian by an exiled Iberian Jew, is carried into Castilian by a man whose first language was Quechua, and he puts that fact on the title page rather than hiding it. He is known in Spanish letters as a translator years before he prints a line about Peru. He is fifty-one.
suggested_refs: La traduzion del indio de los tres Dialogos de amor de Leon Hebreo (Madrid, 1590)
sources: Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, La traduzion del indio (Madrid, 1590)

segments.name: Córdoba, and the Papers That Come Back

stops.name: Córdoba, the permanent move
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1591; the month is not recorded
stops.campa: He leaves Montilla for Córdoba and takes a house near the old mosque the city cut a cathedral into. Here he stays until he dies. Córdoba gives him printers, patrons, and a wider circle of humanists than a country town can hold. He is fifty-two, a captain without a war and a petitioner whose petition failed, and he has not yet written the book. Peru exists for him now entirely in memory: his mother's rooms, the old men's talk, the knotted cords, and the answers his uncle gave a boy who asked.
stops.quote: mi intencion no es contradecirles, sino servirles de comento y glosa, y de interprete en muchos vocablos Indios, que como estrangeros en aquella lengua interpretaron fuera de la propiedad de ella
stops.quote_source: Comentarios Reales de los Incas, prologue 'El autor al lector' (Historia general del Perú, Tomo I, Madrid 1800 ed., Wikisource)
suggested_refs: Garcilaso's house in Córdoba, near the Mezquita-Catedral, his residence from 1591

stops.name: Córdoba, Gonzalo Silvestre at his table
stops.date_confidence: inferred; the interviews are attested by the prologue of La Florida but run across years without dates
stops.campa: He takes down the memory of a veteran named Gonzalo Silvestre, who marched with Hernando de Soto through the interior of Florida and came out of it alive. Over years of talk he checks the old soldier against the written relations and builds La Florida del Inca, a history of a disaster told from inside the column rather than from the commander's dispatches. The method is the one his mother's uncles taught him in Cusco without either party naming it: history is what a witness can still say out loud to somebody who will write it down.
stops.quote: He told many delightful stories about his childhood in Cuzco. But as a historian Garcilaso has forfeited my confidence: he meanders, forgets, romanticises, or blatantly distorts too often to remain authoritative.
stops.quote_source: John Hemming, The Conquest of the Incas (1993 ed.), a modern verdict on the method, cited on en.wikipedia
suggested_refs: La Florida del Inca (1605), prologue naming Gonzalo Silvestre as informant
sources: Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, La Florida del Inca (1605), prologue

stops.name: Santa Cruz, a son lost with Mendaña
stops.date_confidence: the voyage and Mendaña's death at Santa Cruz in October 1595 are attested; the paternity of the man named is not
stops.campa: Álvaro de Mendaña's second Pacific voyage makes the Marquesas and then Santa Cruz, where Mendaña dies in October and the expedition comes apart without ever relocating the Solomon Islands it sailed to find. Among the names attached to the wreck of it is an admiral called Lope de Vega, whom one tradition makes a son of Garcilaso. The paternity is undocumented and the tradition may be nothing at all. A man who never crossed back over his own ocean is said to have lost a son on the far side of another one.
suggested_refs: The second Mendaña expedition of 1595 and its collapse at Santa Cruz (Nendo)

stops.name: Córdoba, the Genealogía de Garci Pérez de Vargas
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1596; the work stayed in manuscript until the twentieth century
stops.campa: He writes out the descent of the Vargas line from Garci Pérez de Vargas, the thirteenth-century knight of the taking of Seville, and does not publish it. The manuscript waits three hundred years for a printer. It is the argument he could not win in the antechambers of Madrid, made at his own desk and for no reader: that his father's blood was what he had always said it was. He proves the Castilian half on paper. The Inca half he proves in print, and to Europe.
suggested_refs: Genealogía de Garci Pérez de Vargas, written 1596, unpublished until the twentieth century

stops.name: Córdoba, the papers of Blas Valera arrive
stops.date_confidence: traditional; the delivery is dated to about 1600, three years after Valera's death at Málaga
stops.campa: Father Pedro Maldonado de Saavedra brings him what was salvaged of the manuscripts of Blas Valera, the Jesuit three years dead at Málaga: torn Latin pages on Inca history and the Quechua language, wrecked, by one account, in the English sack of Cádiz. Valera was the same man made twice, a mestizo of Chachapoyas, son of a conquistador and an Indian mother, silenced by his own order. What he was forbidden to print reaches Córdoba in fragments, and Garcilaso quotes him by name, at length, saying outright that he translates him from the Latin.
stops.quote: tienen en sus acentos casi siempre en la sílaba penúltima
stops.quote_source: Comentarios Reales de los Incas, 'Advertencias acerca de la lengua general de los indios del Perú' (Madrid 1800 ed., Wikisource)
suggested_refs: The surviving fragments of Blas Valera's Historia Occidentalis, delivered to Garcilaso at Córdoba
sources: Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales de los Incas, Libro I cap. VI and Libro V caps. XI-XIV

stops.name: Lisbon, La Florida del Inca printed
stops.date_confidence: attested by the title page imprint; the month is not given
stops.campa: Pedro Crasbeeck prints La Florida del Inca at Lisbon. It is the history of Soto's expedition through the North American southeast, built out of one survivor's spoken memory by a man who has never been within four thousand miles of Florida. He signs it el Inca. The book teaches him what he needs for the far larger one already spread on his table. He learns to weigh witnesses against each other, and to make a European reader trust testimony that arrived by mouth.
suggested_refs: La Florida del Inca (Lisbon: Pedro Crasbeeck, 1605), title page imprint
sources: Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, La Florida del Inca (Lisbon, 1605)

stops.name: Lisbon, the Comentarios Reales printed
stops.date_confidence: attested by the title page imprint; the month is not given
stops.campa: The first part of the Comentarios Reales de los Incas comes off Crasbeeck's press at Lisbon. It lays out the Inca state entire: the succession of the emperors, the roads, the tribute, the religion of the sun, and the quipucamayocs who kept the accounts in knotted cord, told from what he heard in his mother's house and what his schoolfellows sent him from their own mothers' provinces. England will translate it; Spain will ban it in the viceroyalty it describes. Its author is seventy and has not seen Peru in forty-nine years.
stops.quote: Yo protesto decir llanamente la relación que mamé en la leche, y la que después acá he habido, pedida a los propios míos, y prometo que la afición dellos no sea parte para dejar de decir la verdad del hecho.
stops.quote_source: Comentarios Reales de los Incas, Libro I, cap. XIX (Historia general del Perú, Tomo I, Madrid 1800 ed., Wikisource)
suggested_refs: Comentarios Reales de los Incas (Lisbon: Pedro Crasbeeck, 1609), first part
sources: Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, Comentarios Reales de los Incas (Lisbon, 1609)
Wikisource (es), Historia general del Perú, Tomo I

stops.name: Córdoba, the chapel of Las Ánimas bought
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1612; the month is not recorded
stops.campa: He buys the chapel of Las Ánimas del Purgatorio inside the Mezquita-Catedral and endows it as his burial place. The building is a Umayyad mosque with a cathedral cut into the middle of it, horseshoe arches standing over Christian altars, one conquest laid across another and neither one erased. He has spent his working life explaining to Spaniards what it means that Inca stone still holds up the churches of Cusco. He arranges to be buried underneath exactly that argument, in the city where he wrote it out.
suggested_refs: The Capilla de las Ánimas del Purgatorio, Mezquita-Catedral de Córdoba
sources: Cabildo Catedral de Córdoba, chapel records

stops.name: Córdoba, the second part finished
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia dates the completion to about 1613; one summary gives 1612, which appears to be a conflation with the chapel purchase
stops.campa: He finishes the second part of the Comentarios, printed afterwards as the Historia General del Perú: the conquest itself, Cajamarca, the killing of Atahualpa, the wars among the men who took the empire, the executions and risings he watched as a boy in Cusco. He writes about Francisco Pizarro's generation as a man who sat at its elbow taking dictation, and about the Incas as a man whose mother was born to them. Licence and approval are granted and the book goes to press while he is still alive to see the sheets.
suggested_refs: The manuscript of the Historia General del Perú, completed c.1613 and licensed before the author's death

stops.name: Córdoba, the death
stops.date_confidence: the tomb inscription reads 'Fallecio a 22 de abril de 1616'; 23 April is the conventionally cited day and en.wikipedia gives it, es.wikipedia gives a 22-24 April range
stops.campa: He dies in his house in Córdoba, seventy-seven years old, fifty-six of them spent in Spain. The stone cut over him says the twenty-second of April. The date given by convention since is the twenty-third, which is also the day tradition hands, inaccurately, to Cervantes and to Shakespeare. He never went back to Peru and never got the recognition he crossed the ocean to ask for. What he got was not what he travelled for: his mother's family's account of itself, printed in Europe under his own name.
suggested_refs: The house in Córdoba where Garcilaso died in April 1616

stops.name: Mezquita-Catedral, the burial under the arches
stops.date_confidence: the burial day is not recorded in any reachable source; placed immediately after the death the epitaph dates to 22 April 1616
stops.campa: They lay him in his own chapel under the arches of the caliphate. The inscription calls him illustrious in blood, expert in letters, valiant in arms, and gives the three claims in the order he would have chosen, the blood first. It names him Inca on a Spanish tomb inside an Andalusian mosque, which is the whole of his argument compressed into one line of stone. The day of the burial nobody wrote down; the epitaph dates the death, and it is the oldest witness on the question that anyone can still walk in and read.
stops.quote: El Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, varón insigne, digno de perpetua memoria. Ilustre en sangre. Perito en letras. Valiente en armas.
stops.quote_source: Funerary inscription, Capilla de las Ánimas, Mezquita-Catedral de Córdoba, 1616
suggested_refs: The funerary inscription in the Capilla de las Ánimas, Mezquita-Catedral de Córdoba

stops.name: Córdoba, the Historia General del Perú printed
stops.date_confidence: attested by the title page imprint, a year after the author's death
stops.campa: The widow of Andrés de Barrera prints the second part at Córdoba, a year after his death. Its dedication is not to a prince or a patron. It is addressed to the Indians, mestizos, and creoles of Peru, whom he calls his brothers, his countrymen, his own people, from a city not one of them will ever see. The answer an old man gave a boy in a room in Cusco is now a printed book in Andalusia, willed back across the ocean to readers with no press of their own to print it.
stops.quote: A los indios, mestizos y criollos de los reinos y provincias del grande y riquíssimo imperio del Perú, el Inca Garcilasso de la Vega, su hermano, compatriota y paisano, salud y felicidad.
stops.quote_source: Historia General del Perú (Córdoba: viuda de Andrés de Barrera, 1617), dedicatory prologue
suggested_refs: Historia General del Perú (Córdoba: viuda de Andrés de Barrera, 1617), title page imprint
sources: Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, Historia General del Perú (Córdoba, 1617)

segments.name: What the Book Did After Him

stops.name: London, the Royal Commentaries in English
stops.date_confidence: catalogues disagree: the Paul Rycaut entry gives 1688, one Wikipedia article gives 1685; the same article carries a demonstrably wrong date elsewhere
stops.campa: Paul Rycaut, consul at Smyrna and historian of the Ottoman court, puts the Comentarios into English as The Royal Commentaries of Peru. What crosses the Channel is the Inca state as Garcilaso described it: an ordered empire of roads and storehouses and a bureaucracy kept in knotted cord, arriving in the century that is busy inventing the noble savage and will make heavy use of the material. The book is read in England as evidence in an argument its author was not having.
suggested_refs: Paul Rycaut, The Royal Commentaries of Peru (London, 1688)

stops.name: Lima, the book forbidden
stops.date_confidence: attested to 1782, following the Túpac Amaru II rebellion of 1780-81; one extraction gave 1758 for the rising, which is wrong
stops.campa: Túpac Amaru II raises the southern Andes against Spain and is torn apart in the square at Cusco. In the aftermath the crown moves against the reading matter, and a royal order restricts and then forbids the circulation of the Comentarios Reales in the viceroyalty. The book has become what its author never proposed: evidence, in Spanish, that the Incas governed a real state and that their descendants are still in the country. Madrid takes a hundred and seventy years to notice what it licensed.
suggested_refs: The Real Cédula of Carlos III, 1782, restricting the Comentarios Reales in Peru
sources: Historiography of the Túpac Amaru II rebellion

stops.name: Lima, the university takes his name
stops.date_confidence: es.wikipedia gives 21 December 1964; en.wikipedia gives 1965
stops.campa: A private university is founded at Lima and named Universidad Inca Garcilaso de la Vega. The signature he invented at Montilla goes over a lecture hall four centuries later, Inca and Castilian still standing side by side in it. The republic that expelled Spain takes as a founding writer a captain of the Spanish army who died at Córdoba and never came home. He addressed his last book to the Indians, mestizos, and creoles of Peru three centuries before there was a Peru to address.
suggested_refs: Universidad Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, Lima, founded 21 December 1964
sources: Wikipedia (es), 'Universidad Inca Garcilaso de la Vega'

stops.name: Rome, the statue by the Villa Borghese
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the month of the unveiling is not given
stops.campa: A statue of him is set up in Rome beside the gardens of the Villa Borghese. He is honoured in a European capital he never visited, as the first American-born writer of major standing in European letters, a standing established in his own lifetime by a translation of an Italian book. The Neoplatonism he carried into Castilian came off this peninsula. The empire he described in the Comentarios he had already called, in the first page of his prologue, another Rome.
stops.quote: como natural de la ciudad del Cozco, que fue otra Roma en aquel imperio, tengo más larga y clara noticia que la que hasta ahora los escritores han dado
stops.quote_source: Comentarios Reales de los Incas, prologue 'El autor al lector' (1609; text as printed in the Madrid 1800 edition, Wikisource)
suggested_refs: The statue of Inca Garcilaso de la Vega near the Villa Borghese, Rome, 1967
sources: Wikisource (es), Historia general del Perú, Tomo I, 'El autor al lector'

stops.name: Buenos Aires, the companion statue
stops.date_confidence: year attested; the month is not given
stops.campa: A companion figure is raised in Buenos Aires, in a square named for Peru. The two statues stand on opposite shores of the ocean he crossed once and never recrossed: one in the Europe that would not pay his father's wages, one in an America invented long after he died. Nothing in his books anticipates either country. He wrote for the Indians, mestizos, and creoles of a viceroyalty, and the nations that came out of that viceroyalty kept the book and put up the man in bronze.
suggested_refs: The statue of Inca Garcilaso de la Vega, Plaza República del Perú, Buenos Aires, 1973

stops.name: Cusco Cathedral, the ashes returned
stops.date_confidence: attested to 25 November 1978
stops.campa: Juan Carlos I of Spain hands a portion of the ashes back to Cusco, and they are placed in the cathedral on the plaza where the boy was made a Christian in a provisional church three hundred and thirty-nine years before. The rest stays under the arches of the Mezquita, and the division has been argued about ever since. A few streets away, the house on Calle Garcilaso is a museum. He asked the crown once for what was owed him and was refused; the crown came back four centuries later with the only thing it had left.
suggested_refs: The 1978 transfer of a portion of Garcilaso's remains from Córdoba to Cusco Cathedral
